analysis.one_liner: Extends federal online privacy protections from young children to teens and bans targeted advertising to kids.
analysis.headline: The bill won approval from the Senate Commerce Committee and had 22 bipartisan cosponsors, but the Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill amends the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998, which today protects only children under 13. It extends those protections to teens up to age 17, bans companies from collecting kids' and teens' personal information for targeted advertising, adds geolocation and biometric data (like face scans and fingerprints) to the definition of protected personal information, and gives teens and parents the right to see, correct, and delete data collected about them. Enforcement sits with the Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and teens under 17, and their parents. Today, federal privacy law covers websites and apps aimed at children under 13; a 16-year-old has essentially no federal right to stop a platform from profiling them or to delete what has been collected. The bill would give teens the same notice, consent, and deletion rights, and would prohibit companies from building advertising profiles on anyone under 17.

how_it_helps.text: The bill extends the core protections of the 1998 children's online privacy law to teens, defined as individuals over 12 and under 17, requiring operators of sites and apps directed at them (or that know they are collecting data from them) to get consent before collecting personal information.

It makes it unlawful to collect, use, disclose, or compile personal information of a child or teen for purposes of individual-specific advertising — advertising built on personal data, psychological profiling, or device identifiers.
It expands the definition of personal information to include geolocation data and biometric measurements such as fingerprints, voice prints, facial templates, DNA, and gait.

It gives parents of children and teens themselves the right to request a description of what data has been collected, challenge inaccuracies, delete collected data and content they posted, and refuse further collection — with rules preventing operators from cutting off service in retaliation for a deletion request.
It requires operators to collect only information reasonably necessary, set data-retention limits, establish reasonable security practices, and disclose when data is stored outside the United States.

Violations are enforced by the FTC as unfair or deceptive practices, with courts allowed to impose civil penalties above the normal statutory amounts, and state attorneys general may sue on behalf of their residents.

analysis.who_pays: Social media platforms, app developers, and the online advertising industry, which would lose the ability to build behavioral profiles of users under 17 — the data behind a large share of targeted advertising revenue. They would also bear compliance costs for consent systems, deletion requests, and data-minimization rules.
analysis.who_pays_short: Social media, apps, and ad companies

drawbacks.text: The committee-approved version is narrower than what was introduced: it removed connected devices (like smart speakers and connected toys) from the definition of a covered operator and replaced the introduced bill's broad 'targeted marketing' ban with a narrower 'individual-specific advertising' ban, leaving some gaps in coverage.

Verifying users' ages and obtaining consent for sites with mixed audiences could require platforms to collect additional personal information about all users — the very thing privacy laws try to limit.

Compliance costs fall on every operator, including small websites and apps, and ad-supported services aimed at young users could reduce features or restrict access as they rework their business models.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits address a real gap: under existing law a 16-year-old has essentially no federal privacy protections online, and the bill would change that. The costs are real but ordinary — compliance burdens and the loss of targeted-ad revenue from minors — and the strongest objection, that age checks require more data collection, is a design challenge rather than a reason to keep the status quo. The main design criticism is what the bill no longer covers: the committee version dropped connected devices and narrowed the advertising ban compared with the introduced bill.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Commerce Committee approved the bill and put it on the Senate's calendar in December 2023, but the majority leader never called it up for a floor vote, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 3, 2023 by Senator Markey with Senator Cassidy and referred to the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee.
On July 27, 2023, the committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute.

On December 13, 2023, the committee formally reported the bill, and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 288 — meaning it was awaiting floor time, not awaiting committee work.

The committee substitute narrowed the introduced bill: it removed connected devices from the definition of a covered operator and replaced the introduced bill's broad ban on 'targeted marketing' with a narrower ban on 'individual-specific advertising.'
No further action was ever taken, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 without a Senate vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies whose revenue depends on collecting and monetizing data about children and teens — online advertising firms, social media platforms, and app operators — kept a status quo in which teens have essentially no federal privacy rights. Senators had already moved the bill through committee at no cost to themselves by voting for it there.

for.name: Edward Markey
for.role: U.S. Senator (D-MA), bill sponsor and author of the original 1998 children's privacy law
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and guided it through the Senate Commerce Committee.

for.name: Bill Cassidy
for.what_they_did: Joined Markey in introducing the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship from day one.

for.name: Maria Cantwell
for.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill favorably out of committee with a substitute amendment and had it placed on the Senate calendar.

for.name: 22 Senate cosponsors
for.role: Bipartisan bloc of cosponsors (8 Republicans, 13 Democrats, 1 independent)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill bipartisan backing in the Senate.

against.name: Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a Senate floor vote during the roughly 13 months it sat on the Senate calendar.

against.name: Online advertising and tech industry groups
against.role: Adtech, social media, and app industry trade associations
against.what_they_did: Opposed children's and teens' online privacy legislation, which would end behavioral advertising to minors — their core data-driven revenue model.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan from the start — 13 Democrats, 8 Republicans, and 1 independent cosponsored, and the Senate Commerce Committee reported it favorably — but no floor vote was ever taken, so no party breakdown exists on the merits.

industries.note: The bill makes it unlawful to collect, use, disclose, or compile personal information of anyone under 17 for individual-specific advertising — the behavioral profiling and tracking that underpin the adtech business model. Its interest in this bill ran against the public's interest in keeping minors' data out of ad profiles.

industries.industry: Social media platforms and app operators
industries.note: Platforms would face consent requirements, deletion rights, data-minimization and security mandates, and FTC/state enforcement with elevated civil penalties. They would keep operating under the framework — and the committee version actually eased their exposure by exempting connected devices — but they would lose the ability to profile and target users under 17.

industries.industry: Connected device makers (smart speakers, connected toys, wearables)
industries.note: The committee-approved version removed 'connected device' from the definition of a covered operator, exempting this whole product category from the bill even though such devices collect data from children. That carve-out came out of the markup process.
